text.p: Saudi Arabia's industrial and petrochemical giant Saudi Basic Industries Corp (SABIC) said it has mandated a consortium of banks to arrange a $850 million syndicated loan for one of its affiliates.

A SABIC statement said the deal was signed on November 12 with local, regional and international banks to help finance petrochemical projects by the Industrial Fibres Company (Ibn Rushd), owned by SABIC as well as Saudi and Bahraini firms.

It named the banks as Riyadh-based Arab National Bank -- owned by Amman-based Arab Bank along with Saudi Arabia's Riyad Bank, Bahrain-based Gulf International Bank, JP Morgan, Britain's Barclays Bank Plc, Industrial Bank of Japan, The Arab Petroleum Investments Corp (APICORP) and Saudi Cairo Bank.

Bankers in the Gulf this week told Reuters the eight banks -- who are equal arrangers -- had received the mandate earlier in the month and had been waiting for a final word from Ibn Rushd before starting preparations for the syndication.

They said the consortium will approach regional and international banks to take part in the syndication and did not foresee any problems in raising the loan since Ibn Rushd had a "good reputation" and was affiliated to SABIC, seen as a profit-making giant.

"We are pleased that the national, regional and international banks have come forward to fund this project which is extremely important for the national economy of Saudi Arabia," said the SABIC statement, received by Reuters.

Ibn Rushd will use the loan to finance the construction of a 350,000-tonnes per year purified terephthalic acid (PTA) plant -- due to come on stream in 1997 -- as well as a world-scale aromatic plant -- which would produce 350,000 metric tonnes of benzene and 300,000 metric tonnes of paraxylene a year. It will also produce orthoxylene and metaxylene and is due to come on stream by early 1998.

Saudi Arabia is expanding and opening up its petrochemical sector to private finance in an attempt to diversify its oil-dominated economy. New multi-million dollar petrochemical plants feeding off the country's abundant gas reserves are expected to come on stream until early into the next decade.
